slides.title: What is Soroban?

items.label: Stellar's smart contract platform
items.text: built into the core protocol, not a sidechain.

items.label: Live on mainnet
items.text: since February 20, 2024 (Protocol 20); opened to public dApp deployment in March 2024.

items.label: Rust → WASM
items.text: contracts are written in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly and executed by Stellar Core.

items.label: Beyond payments
items.text: extends a payments-first network to DeFi and other financial services.

blocks.text: Not EVM-compatible: it is a separate design, so Solidity habits do not carry over directly.

slides.notes: Sources: eco.com Soroban overview (launch dates), The Block (March 2024 launch coverage).

slides.title: Core idea 1 — Rust → WASM

blocks.text: Soroban contracts are written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (WASM) — a portable, sandboxed bytecode format that runs efficiently on any platform.

items.label: Why Rust?
items.text: Memory safety, strong typing, and excellent tooling. Rust prevents entire classes of bugs common in smart contracts (buffer overflows, null pointer dereferences).

items.label: Why WASM?
items.text: Deterministic execution (same output on any machine), small binary size, and fast validation. The Stellar network can execute WASM without trusting the compiler.

items.label: Build process
items.text: Use stellar contract build, not cargo build. This targets wasm32v1-none and optimizes for the Soroban environment.

items.label: SDK versioning
items.text: The soroban-sdk tracks Stellar protocol versions. SDK v28 works with Protocol 28, ensuring your contract uses the right host features.

blocks.text: Result: Your contract compiles to a ~50-200KB WASM file that anyone can upload to Stellar and execute deterministically.

slides.notes: Rust's ownership model prevents data races. WASM is standardized by W3C and supported by major browsers and blockchains.

slides.title: Core idea 2 — The Env

blocks.text: Every contract function receives an Env parameter — your only interface to the Stellar host (the blockchain runtime). Think of Env as the syscall layer between your code and the network.

items.label: What Env provides
items.text: Storage (read/write data), cryptography (hashing, signing), events (logging), authorization (verify signatures), and ledger info (current block, timestamp).

items.label: Why #![no_std]?
items.text: Contracts cannot use the Rust standard library. No file I/O, no networking, no system calls. This ensures contracts are deterministic and sandboxed.

items.label: SDK types are required
items.text: Use Soroban's Symbol, Vec, Map, Address, String, Bytes instead of std types. These are optimized for the WASM environment and integrate with storage.

items.label: Example usage
items.text: env.storage().persistent().get(&key) reads from contract storage. env.crypto().sha256(&data) hashes data. env.current_contract_address() gets your contract's address.

blocks.text: The Env pattern means your contract is pure logic — all side effects go through the host, which can meter, validate, and record them.

slides.notes: This design is similar to Solana's accounts model but more explicit. Env is passed to every function, making dependencies clear.

slides.title: Core idea 3 — Storage tiers & state archival

blocks.text: Soroban has three storage tiers with different costs and behaviors. Unlike Ethereum (where state lives forever), Soroban state has a Time-To-Live (TTL) and must be renewed.

rows: Small contract config (admin, token name, metadata)
Archived with contract (auto-restore on contract use)
Archived — must be manually restored before reading

items.label: Why this design?
items.text: Prevents state bloat. On Ethereum, all historical state grows forever. Soroban's archival system keeps the ledger small and fast.

items.label: TTL management
items.text: Call extend_ttl(threshold, extend_to) to renew storage. Threshold = minimum remaining ledgers before renewal, extend_to = new TTL in ledgers.

items.label: Archival vs deletion
items.text: Archived data is moved to cheaper storage and can be restored. Temporary data is gone forever — use for truly ephemeral values.

blocks.text: Critical: If you don't extend TTLs, users' balances could become inaccessible. Design your contract to auto-extend on key operations.

slides.notes: This is the biggest difference from Ethereum. Accessed via env.storage().instance() / .persistent() / .temporary(). One ledger ≈ 5 seconds.

slides.title: Core idea 4 — Authorization

blocks.text: Soroban has a built-in authorization system. Instead of manually checking msg.sender like in Solidity, you declare which addresses must authorize a function call.

items.label: How it works
items.text: Call address.require_auth() in your function. The Stellar host checks that the transaction includes a valid signature from that address.

items.label: Universal auth
items.text: Works identically for classic Stellar accounts (ed25519 keys) and contract accounts (smart contracts can authorize actions too).

items.label: Scoped permissions
items.text: require_auth() can be scoped to specific functions and arguments. Users approve exactly what they're signing, not blanket permissions.

items.label: Security benefits
items.text: No hand-rolled auth logic means fewer bugs. The host handles signature verification, replay protection, and nonce management.

items.label: Example
items.text: fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: u64) { from.require_auth(); ... } — only 'from' can authorize this transfer.

blocks.text: This is similar to Ethereum's msg.sender pattern but more explicit and type-safe. The host enforces it, not your contract code.

slides.notes: Source: SDF blog, 'Soroban: the smart contract platform designed for developers'. Soroban auth is inspired by Stellar's existing multi-sig and op auth patterns.

slides.title: Core idea 5 — Native assets in contracts

blocks.text: Stellar has a native asset system (XLM and custom tokens). Soroban doesn't create new tokens — it lets smart contracts interact with existing Stellar assets through the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC).

items.label: What is the SAC?
items.text: A built-in smart contract that wraps any Stellar asset (XLM, USDC, custom tokens). It's deployed once per asset and provides a standard token interface.

items.label: SEP-41 interface
items.text: The SAC implements SEP-41, Stellar's equivalent to ERC-20. Methods like approve, allowance, transfer, transfer_from, balance, mint, burn.

items.label: No bridges needed
items.text: Your contract moves real Stellar assets, not wrapped versions. If you send USDC in a Soroban contract, it's actual USDC on Stellar, not a bridged copy.

items.label: Issuer rules still apply
items.text: Trustlines, authorization flags, and issuer controls from classic Stellar still work. The SAC enforces these rules at the contract level.

items.label: Example usage
items.text: let token = Address::from_contract_id(&sac_id); token_client::allowance(&env, &token, &owner, &spender) checks an allowance.

blocks.text: This means Soroban DeFi can use the same assets that exist in Stellar's payment ecosystem — unified liquidity, no fragmentation.

slides.notes: The SAC is a core contract deployed by the protocol. You don't deploy it yourself — you just reference existing asset contracts.

slides.title: Core idea 6 — Resource-based fees

blocks.text: Soroban fees are based on actual resource usage (CPU, memory, I/O), not gas. You simulate first, declare resources, then pay exactly what you declared. No gas auctions, no surprise fees.

items.title: Step 1: Simulate
items.text: Call RPC simulateTransaction with your transaction. The host runs it without committing and measures: CPU instructions, memory bytes, storage reads/writes, and ledger footprint.

items.title: Step 2: Declare
items.text: Include the measured resources in your transaction (cpu_instructions, memory_bytes, etc.). This is your resource budget.

items.title: Step 3: Pay
items.text: Submit the transaction. You pay fees based on your declared resources, regardless of actual usage (up to the limit). Costs are predictable and bounded.

items.label: Why this model?
items.text: Ethereum's gas system has unpredictable fees during congestion. Soroban's resource model gives deterministic pricing — you know the cost before submitting.

items.label: Resource types
items.text: CPU (computation), Memory (RAM), Storage I/O (reads/writes), Ledger footprint (new entries). Each has a base fee per unit.

items.label: No gas auctions
items.text: Fees don't spike based on network demand. If you declare enough resources, your transaction will include at the known fee.

items.label: Client responsibility
items.text: Your frontend or SDK must simulate before submitting. The stellar-cli and JS SDK handle this automatically.

blocks.text: If you declare too few resources, the transaction fails. If you declare too many, you overpay but the transaction succeeds. Best practice: use simulation results directly.

slides.notes: Simulation is a required step in any client flow. The resource model is inspired by AWS Lambda and other serverless pricing models.

slides.title: Workflow with the Stellar CLI

blocks.content:
# 1. Scaffold a workspace
stellar contract init my-project

# 2. Compile to .wasm
stellar contract build

# 3. Create and fund a testnet identity
stellar keys generate alice --network testnet --fund

# 4. Deploy
stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/counter.wasm \
  --source alice --network testnet

# 5. Invoke
stellar contract invoke --id <CONTRACT_ID> \
  --source alice --network testnet \
  -- increment --caller alice

slides.notes: keys generate --fund uses Friendbot on testnet to fund the new account.
